## [Disagreements surface over renovation of historic building housing the Territorial Registrar’s Office](https://www.samoanews.com/local-news/disagreements-surface-over-renovation-historic-building-housing-territorial-registrars)

via Samoa News · 2026-11-13

[![endering of the proposed perimeter fence](https://www.samoanews.com/sites/default/files/styles/slideshow/public/field/image/territorial_registrars_office_0.jpg?itok=5EZWANXD)](https://www.samoanews.com/sites/default/files/styles/article_normal_image/public/field/image/territorial_registrars_office_0.jpg?itok=kYI4J2Cj)

By

Asi Andrew Fa'asau

andrew@samoanews.com

_Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA —_ One of the few remaining landmark structures from the U.S. Naval Administration era in American Samoa is currently undergoing renovation as efforts continue to preserve an important piece of the territory's history. The project also includes plans to construct a fence around the building to tackle a longstanding litter problem beneath its surrounding awning.

And, while the PNRS Board approved the proposed improvements, the debate has highlighted the enduring importance of preserving one of American Samoa's last remaining links to the U.S. Naval Administration era and ensuring that any changes made today respect its historical significance for generations to come.

**THE RENOVATION PROJECT**

Located in the heart of downtown Fagatogo, it was originally constructed in 1917 during the Naval Administration period as a U.S. Navy radio communications station. The facility played a vital role in maintaining communications between American Samoa and other U.S. military and government outposts across the Pacific.

The historic building is now home to the Office of the Territorial Registrar, a division of the Department of Legal Affairs under the Attorney General's Office.

Last week, Attorney General Gwen Tauiliili-Langkilde appeared before a public hearing of the Project Notification and Review System (PNRS) Board to seek approval for additional improvements to be incorporated into an existing land-use permit for the project.

The Attorney General told board members that the project is being carried out in two phases. She explained that Phase One, which is already underway, focuses on renovating and restoring the interior of the historic building. Phase Two would involve improvements to the exterior, including the installation of a new roof, the addition of a gutter system, and the construction of a perimeter fence.

According to Tauiliili-Langkilde, the exterior upgrades are intended to complement the ongoing interior restoration while helping to preserve the building's long-term structural integrity. She noted that the improvements would provide greater protection from the elements, help prevent rainwater damage, and reduce future maintenance needs.

With regard to the re-roofing component of the project, the Attorney General told board members that the existing roof is deteriorating and requires upgrading with stronger, more durable roofing materials capable of withstanding the Territory's harsh weather conditions.

She noted that there are currently open spaces beneath the eaves that allow rain, wind, and pests, including rats and other rodents, to enter the structure. Closing these gaps, she said, would help protect the building from deterioration while improving its overall security and preservation.

Tauiliili-Langkilde also explained that the installation of a gutter system is an important component of the proposed exterior improvements because the building currently has no gutters to collect and channel rainwater. As a result, water runoff flows directly from the roof onto the surrounding area, increasing the risk of water damage over time. The proposed gutter system would redirect rainwater into the existing drainage network, helping to protect both the building and its foundation.

In explaining the proposed fence, she noted it would enhance security and assist in addressing the persistent littering problem around the property.

The sheltered area beneath the building's surrounding awning has become a popular gathering spot for travelers arriving and departing on inter-island ferries to Manu'a and Apia, as well as those waiting to be picked up by family members or transportation providers. Officials say the persistent accumulation of trash in the area prompted the Governor's Office to include the fence as part of the building's improvement and preservation efforts.

Tauiliili-Langkilde further emphasized that the property is situated in one of the busiest and most heavily congested areas of Fagatogo.

The building faces the main roadway into the downtown area and is flanked by the access road leading to the inter-island ferry wharf. In addition, a secondary access road runs behind the structure and is frequently used by vehicles delivering or collecting cargo, packages, and pallets of goods.

Tauiliili-Langkilde told board members that the proposed fence would help establish a clear boundary around the historic property, improve security, and protect the building from damage caused by the high volume of vehicle and pedestrian traffic. She added that the fence would also help preserve the site's appearance and integrity while complementing the broader restoration effort aimed at safeguarding one of the Territory's historic landmarks.

**PUBLIC CONCERNS**

Plans to install a perimeter fence around the building drew the strongest criticism from several members of the public, who argued that such a feature would detract from the historic character and visual appeal of the landmark. Opponents contended that enclosing the structure with a fence would make it resemble a mausoleum or secured compound, diminishing its prominence and aesthetic value in the heart of the town.

One staunch critic, Jim McGuire, a longtime resident who is currently a member of the Zoning Board, described the justification for the proposed fence as superficial and unconvincing. According to McGuire, concerns about travelers using the area beneath the building's awning as a waiting area could be addressed through simpler and more practical measures that would not compromise the building's appearance.

"The government is looking at spending a substantial amount of money on a fence that may not even solve the underlying issue," he said. "A far more practical and cost-effective solution would be for the Registrar's Office to hire a casual worker whose responsibility would be to keep the grounds and surrounding area clean and well maintained. The office could also install signs reminding people not to litter and provide adequate trash bins for public use. It's really that simple.

"Instead of spending taxpayer dollars on a fence that could detract from the appearance of one of American Samoa's historic landmarks, the government should focus on basic maintenance and public awareness. Keeping the area clean, providing proper waste disposal facilities, and ensuring regular upkeep would address the problem without compromising the beauty and historical character of the building."

McGuire, who attended the PNRS public hearing as a member of the public, argued that the historic building should remain as open and visible to the public as possible. He said that, as one of the few surviving structures from the U.S. Naval Administration era, it should not be surrounded by barriers that could diminish public access to and appreciation of an important part of American Samoa's history.

When PNRS Board Chairman Tino Ma'o gave members of the public and the media the opportunity to ask questions about the proposed project, McGuire asked the attorney general whether the proposal should be referred first to the Zoning Board for consideration, arguing that the PNRS Board's primary focus is environmental and land-use matters.

He also noted that the board's eight members are government representatives and questioned whether there had been sufficient public input on a proposal affecting one of the Territory's most significant historic landmarks.

"As I mentioned, that building has been there since 1917," the AG responded. "It was there first. If anything, anything new around it needs to go to the Zoning Board. That building was the first on the block, so to speak."

McGuire also argued that the Office of the Territorial Registrar should be relocated to a safer location on higher ground, away from areas vulnerable to flooding during heavy rainfall or natural disasters such as tsunamis. He pointed out that the building was flooded during the last tsunami, damaging priceless legal documents kept there. He said it has never been disclosed how much it cost the government to send the water-damaged files off-island to be dry-frozen in an attempt to save the ink.

"The Office of the Territorial Registrar is entrusted with preserving some of the Territory's most important historical and legal records, so it should be housed in a facility that offers greater protection from natural hazards," he said. "A more suitable location would be the Lumana'i Building directly across the street."

Responding to this suggestion, AG Tauiliili-Langkilde pointed out that the Lumana'i Building is "privately, semi-autonomously owned" by the American Samoa Development Bank.

"So if we move the Territorial Registrar's Office to the Lumana'i Building, people like you who have used that building since 1975 and me, who have used it since 1993, will have to pay more fees for the use of that building because it's not going to be free," the attorney general explained.

In an interview with McGuire after the hearing, he admitted that he forgot to point out to AG Tauiliili-Langkilde that the Lumana'i Building is owned by a government entity, so it should be possible to negotiate a reduced rental rate in recognition of the vital public service provided by the Registrar's Office.

"Unlike other government agencies, it is not a major revenue-generating office, yet it is responsible for safeguarding records that are of immense historical, legal, and cultural importance to the Territory," McGuire argued. "Those records deserve to be protected in a location that is secure, accessible, and better equipped to withstand natural disasters.

"The ideal government agency to occupy the building is the American Samoa Visitors Bureau, which is currently leasing office space in Tedi's Building," he said. "Given its location along the main road and adjacent to the Main Wharf, this historic structure would serve as a perfect home for the Visitors Bureau."

He argued that the building's strategic location makes it a natural point of contact for tourists arriving by sea, particularly during cruise ship visits.

"When a cruise ship is in port, passengers typically disembark and walk directly into town. The first place many of them would look for information, directions, and visitor services is the Visitors Bureau," he explained. "Having the bureau located in this historic building would not only provide greater visibility and accessibility for visitors, but it would also breathe new life into the structure and give it a purpose that complements its historical significance."

According to McGuire, converting the building into a tourism information center would create a more welcoming gateway to the Territory while preserving public access to one of American Samoa's most recognizable historic landmarks.

"Instead of fencing it off and limiting its interaction with the public, the building could become a showcase for American Samoa's culture, history, and tourism attractions," he said. "It would be a fitting use for such a prominent and historic property, while the Territorial Registrar's Office could be relocated to a safer and more secure facility better suited for protecting important government records.

"After welcoming visitors to the Territory, the Visitors Bureau staff could share the history of American Samoa as an unincorporated territory of the United States and explain how it was initially administered by the U.S. Navy," he said. "They could then tell the story of the building itself and the important role it played in maintaining communications between American Samoa and other U.S. military and government outposts throughout the Pacific."

He noted that the building's historical significance extends beyond its architectural value and is tied directly to events that helped shape the Territory's history.

Among the stories that could be highlighted, he noted, are the building's vital function as a communications hub during the U.S. Naval Administration, its role in helping authorities respond to the 1918 influenza pandemic, and its participation in the network of radio communications used during the search for famed aviator Amelia Earhart following her disappearance in 1937.

"These are the kinds of stories that visitors would find fascinating," he continued. "They highlight the important role this building and the communications network associated with it played in the history of American Samoa and the wider Pacific. Preserving that history and sharing it with visitors would be a far more meaningful use of the building than simply surrounding it with a fence."

McGuire concluded by urging government officials to postpone any decision on the proposed perimeter fence until a broader public discussion can be held.

He suggested that representatives from the Historic Preservation Office, Port Administration, the American Samoa Visitors Bureau, the Arts Council, preservation organizations, and the public should have an opportunity to weigh in on the long-term future of the historic property before permanent changes are made.

**HISTORIC PRESERVATION OFFICE**

Samoa News reached out to Tish Peau, Territorial Archaeologist with the Historic Preservation Office (HPO), to explain why she supported the Department of Legal Affairs' request to construct a perimeter fence around the historic building.

According to Peau, her office approved the request because the proposed fence would be a temporary measure until funding becomes available for a future project to raise the building to street level. She explained that when the structure was originally built, it sat at the same grade as the surrounding area. Over time, however, roadwork, development, and natural changes in the landscape caused the surrounding ground level to rise, leaving the building lower than its surroundings and more vulnerable to litter and drainage problems.

Peau said the temporary fence, combined with the proposed roof replacement and gutter installation, would help protect the historic structure from the elements and address the longstanding litter problem while longer-term preservation plans are developed.

McGuire, however, strongly disagreed with the proposal to elevate the building in the future.

"I think the idea of raising this historic building three or four feet off the ground is unrealistic," he said. "In more than 20 years of real estate appraisal experience in American Samoa and California, I have never seen a historic concrete-foundation building lifted that far. The only practical way to do it would be to dismantle the structure and reconstruct it on a higher foundation in its original form, and that would be extremely expensive."

Born in 1928 in Russia’s Maritime Province, Shin was just nine years old when Joseph Stalin’s regime forcibly relocated roughly 172,000 ethnic Koreans from the Soviet Far East to Central Asia on unsubstantiated suspicions of espionage for Imperial Japan. Packed into cattle cars for a grueling weeks-long journey, thousands perished along the way. Shin survived the ordeal and went on to study art in Uzbekistan, building a career there while dedicating his brush to bearing witness to the trauma of displacement and the resilience of ethnic Koreans rebuilding their lives in an unfamiliar land. His signature “Requiem” series confronts the sorrow of losing a homeland while honoring the victims and celebrating human dignity amid hardship. ## [Dust from unpaved roads creates health hazard for students, faipule warns](https://www.samoanews.com/local-news/dust-unpaved-roads-creates-health-hazard-students-faipule-says)

via Samoa News · 2026-11-12

[![unpaved road](https://www.samoanews.com/sites/default/files/styles/slideshow/public/field/image/2202.jpg?itok=i89xAOlB)](https://www.samoanews.com/sites/default/files/styles/article_normal_image/public/field/image/2202.jpg?itok=03bvnfEy)

By

Samoa News staff

reporters@samoanews.com

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA —  Representative Fagaima Larry Sanitoa has reached out to ASDOE director Maefau Dr. Mary Taufete'e on behalf of several local families and parents requesting a site visit or a meeting regarding the school bus route on Ottoville Road, specifically for students residing in the area behind the Pagofie home.

He points out that currently, about a hundred families live in this neighborhood, and points out that due to the dry and windy weather, the unpaved road generates significant dust, creating a health hazard for students walking home.

The Tualauta faipule notes that he understands that this secondary access road is already included under the CIP plan, and will be repaired eventually.

In the meantime, the concerned families and parents are asking that the school bus drivers drive further into the neighborhood to drop students off closer to their homes.

Fagaima says that additionally, he is coordinating with Vailu'u & Sons Construction (which has a storage area along this road) and ASPA to see if the road can be watered down regularly to help mitigate the dust.

## [DMWR’s two new vessels christened — the Ta'io and Sausauimoana II](https://www.samoanews.com/local-news/dmwrs-two-new-vessels-christened-taio-and-sausauimoana-ii)

via Samoa News · 2026-11-12

[![DMWR enforcement vessel Sausauimoana II christened](https://www.samoanews.com/sites/default/files/styles/slideshow/public/field/image/img_7520.jpg?itok=TI8wqoev)](https://www.samoanews.com/sites/default/files/styles/article_normal_image/public/field/image/img_7520.jpg?itok=M-p6Kknc)

By

Asi Andrew Fa'asau

andrew@samoanews.com

_Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA —_ The Department of Marine and Wildlife Resources (DMWR) marked a significant milestone last Friday with the christening of two new vessels that will strengthen the department's ability to protect American Samoa's marine resources and support fisheries management throughout the Territory.

The ceremony brought Lieutenant Governor Pulumataala Ae Ae Jr., government officials, community partners, DMWR personnel, and invited guests together to celebrate the addition of the Ta'io and Sausauimoana II to the department's operational fleet.

The expansion of the fleet represents an important investment in DMWR's ongoing efforts to safeguard the Territory's vast marine environment, enforce fisheries regulations, and conduct critical field operations in local waters.

Among the highlights of the ceremony was the christening of the Ta'io, a state-of-the-art safe boat manufactured by Safe Boats International, a company based in Seattle. Designed for durability, reliability, and performance in challenging ocean conditions, the vessel is 38 feet long and 12 feet wide and will enhance DMWR's ability to conduct offshore patrols, marine research activities, and emergency response operations.

Present at the christening ceremony was Safe Boats International representative Yehudah Landau, who traveled here for the occasion and will be conducting training for DMWR staff on how to operate the boat.

In an exclusive interview with DMWR Director Nathan Ilaoa, he explained that the new vessel Taʻio was named after the Tahiti Petrel, a rare seabird found in American Samoa that is known for its ability to travel vast distances across the Pacific Ocean, but always finds its way back to its nesting grounds on the mountains of Tutuila. The name reflects the vessel's mission of safeguarding the Territory's marine resources and supporting conservation efforts throughout local waters.

Joining the Ta'io in the fleet is the 32-foot-long enforcement vessel Sausauimoana II, constructed locally through a partnership with Industrial Gases. The boat has been specially customized to support fisheries inspections and monitoring activities, providing DMWR officers with an additional platform for carrying out their regulatory and conservation responsibilities. According to longtime businessman Peter Crispin, the vessel took about three months to build with assistance from Andy Wearing.

Officials noted that the acquisition of the two vessels comes at a critical time as DMWR continues its work to combat illegal fishing activities, monitor fishing fleets, collect scientific data, and ensure the sustainable management of marine resources that are vital to the Territory's economy, food security, and cultural heritage. The Ta'io was purchased with ARPA funds totaling about $900,000, while the Sausauimoana II was purchased with funds from the NOAA Fisheries Office of Law Enforcement.

Speaking during the ceremony, leaders emphasized that the new additions will improve the department's operational reach and increase its ability to respond efficiently to issues affecting local fisheries and marine ecosystems throughout the year.

The vessels are expected to play a key role in supporting inspections, enforcement efforts, marine conservation programs, and resource management initiatives in waters surrounding Tutuila, Aunu'u, Manu'a, Swains Island, and other areas under the Territory's jurisdiction.

The event also highlighted the importance of partnerships between government agencies and private-sector organizations in strengthening American Samoa's marine resource management capabilities.

DMWR Director Ilaoa and his staff were recognized for their efforts in securing and overseeing the acquisition of the vessels, which officials described as a major achievement for the department.

As the ceremony concluded, guests gathered to offer congratulations and blessings for the crews who will operate the vessels and the important work they will carry out in protecting the Territory's ocean resources for future generations.

The christening of the Ta'io and Sausauimoana II signals another step forward in DMWR's mission to conserve American Samoa's marine environment while ensuring that the Territory's fisheries remain healthy, productive, and sustainable for years to come.

Spicy instant noodles may offer a temporary sense of stress relief, but the fiery kick that makes it appealing can also trigger heartburn, abdominal pain and other digestive discomfort, particularly for people with sensitive stomachs. Capsaicin, the compound responsible for the burning sensation in chili peppers, stimulates pain receptors and can prompt the release of endorphins, chemicals involved in the body's response to pain. While this reaction may help explain why some people feel better after eating spicy food, the sensation of relief does not necessarily mean the food is beneficial to their health. The potential health effects have drawn renewed attention following a Korea Consumer Agency (KCA) report examining 12 popular instant noodle products sold in Korea. ## [Behavioral Health, Drug & Rehabilitation Center Project needs extension to complete](https://www.samoanews.com/local-news/behavioral-health-drug-rehabilitation-center-project-needs-extension-complete)

via Samoa News · 2026-11-10

[![Behavioral Health & Drug and Alcohol Rehabilitation Clinic construction site](https://www.samoanews.com/sites/default/files/styles/slideshow/public/field/image/3908.jpg?itok=feHz4rPl)](https://www.samoanews.com/sites/default/files/styles/article_normal_image/public/field/image/3908.jpg?itok=1ax4b3AO)

By

Samoa News staff

reporters@samoanews.com

_Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA —_ House Representative (Faipule) Fagaima Larry Sanitoa’s request to Congresswoman Uifa’atali Aumua Amata for urgent assistance to help the territory obtain deadline extensions for ARPA funds through legislative help did not include specifics about the ARPA-funded projects that are at risk.

The projects are facing a looming December 31, 2026 deadline — to be completed or lose the remaining funding.

Samoa News has learned that one of the projects Fagaima has been asked to help, is the Department of Health (DOH) Behavioral Health, Drug and Rehabilitation Center Project, being built in Tafuna (in the old Tafuna Housing area).

The DOH ARPA Senior Projects manager, on behalf of DOH director Dr. Saipale Fuimaono, prepared a summary report for Fagaima, and provided photos to verify the construction site’s progress or condition to help its request to get an extension.

The report, dated October 13, 2026, an excel document, shows that the overall project is 70% completed. It indicates that delays have been due to shipping, Acts of God, and weather conditions, and lays out that the project’s Phase 6 through 11 are scheduled to be completed in May 2027.

DOH ARPA Senior Projects Manager Falanai M. Ala includes a professional observation or opinion of the construction work. He writes:

The Silva Group has been working very hard at moving this project to its completion. They have worked 7 days a week, and utilizing night shifts when they pour concrete during the Foundation, Slab on Grade, and Brick Laying phases’ many days.

They have been averaging approximately 65 to 75 workers on site daily and sometimes 100 workers  during big concrete pours.  They also have a night crew working on an "as needed basis" during the concrete pours, brick laying, and other construction phases.

The Silva Group is definitely one of the best Contractors the DOH has on its ARPA Construction Projects.  This project is progressing according to schedule, despite all of the difficulty in shipping, work force, and weather delays. This project is approximately 70% overall complete.

The Silva Group has not submitted a single change order as of 10/14/26, considering the fact that this project was design by a third party Architectural Firm name, Jacob Cubitt Architects (JCA) in Australia, through PIOA Consultants.

This is very un-usual and rare for contractors in American Samoa to construct a building this far into the construction process without submitting any change order for the project.

The only change order we are anticipating for this project is the purchase and installation price for the stand-by generator for the BHS Facility. This was not included in the Request for Proposal (RFP) and Scope of work (SOW).

The Silva Group is a company with integrity and high moral character, they treat their employees very well.

He concludes that “the DOH ARPA Team is extremely proud and happy to work with the Silva Group on this project.“

Reported elsewhere in today’s edition, Congresswoman Amata, who is now in Washington D.C. is an update of her efforts to extend the deadline for ARPA funding legislatively, and includes writing a letter to U.S. Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent asking for his support.

Gov. Pulaali’i Nikolao Pula made his own request in October 2026 to the U.S. Department of the Treasury for a six-month extension to complete the American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) projects.

Amata in her comments on the issue, reminded Samoa News that this is the second time an extension for completion has been requested for ARPA funding, the first request occurred in 2025, which led to the current deadline of December 31, 2026.

## [Honoring those who have worn our country’s uniform](https://www.samoanews.com/local-news/honoring-those-who-have-worn-our-countrys-uniform)

via Samoa News · 2026-11-10

[![Veterans Day banner](https://www.samoanews.com/sites/default/files/styles/slideshow/public/field/image/veterans_day_banner.png?itok=_1QgC01r)](https://www.samoanews.com/sites/default/files/styles/article_normal_image/public/field/image/veterans_day_banner.png?itok=59evZ2Jc)

By

Samoa News staff

reporters@samoanews.com

_Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA —_ In observance of Veterans Day, Governor Pulaalii Nikolai Pula has declared Wednesday, November 11, 2026 a public holiday in American Samoa. All ASG offices will be closed, with normal government operation resuming on Thursday, November 12, 2026,  Department directors and agency heads are reminded to ensure essential government services remain operational as necessary.

“On behalf of Lieutenant Governor Pulumataala and the Administration, we express our sincere gratitude to all veterans and their families, particularly our sons and daughters, for their service and sacrifice. We honor the courage and dedication of those who served in United States Armed Forces to defend our nation and uphold our freedoms. Happy Veterans Day! God bless our veterans, and God bless American Samoa,” Governor Pulaali i Nikolao Pula said in general memorandum issued over the weekend.

Congresswoman Uifa’atali Aumua Amata who serves as Vice Chairman of the House Veterans’ Affairs Committee is honoring U.S. Veterans and especially thanking American Samoa’s Veterans this Veterans Day.

“Thank you to our Veterans, and have a blessed Veterans Day. You mean so much to our islands, and we appreciate your leadership and wisdom,” said Congresswoman Amata. “I am humbled to serve our Veterans on the Committee, where we constantly hear from our Veterans and work for improved performance from the VA, based on that input from Veterans and Service Organizations.

“Thank you to each one for your service and patriotism,” continued Amata. “ As a nation, we have made an enduring national commitment to all our veterans for their care and wellbeing, at every age. This includes their healthcare, assisting transitions out of the Armed Forces, furthering their second careers or higher education, to hospice, burial services and dignified funeral honors, as well as survivor benefits and comfort. Our Veterans should know their families are secure.

“Like so many of us in American Samoa, my father and brothers served, and we love and honor our Veterans and our military families. May God protect our Service Members, and bless and uphold our Veterans.”

On Monday, the House was scheduled to vote on the bipartisan Veterans’ Compensation Cost-of-Living Adjustment Act of 2026. The bill increases the rates of compensation for veterans with service-connected disabilities, and the rates of dependency and indemnity compensation for the survivors of certain disabled veterans.

The US Postal Service Office and the Territorial Bank of American Samoa will be closed in observance of Veterans Day, tomorrow.

In honor of Veterans Day, Samoa News offices will also be closed and there will be no Wednesday issue. Samoa News will finish out the week with issues on Thursday and Friday.

**BACKGROUND**

Originally established as Armistice Day in 1919 by President Woodrow Wilson to mark the first anniversary of the end of World War I (hostilities formally ceased on the 11th hour of the 11th day of the 11th month in 1918).

Renamed Veterans Day in 1954 under President Dwight D. Eisenhower to honor all American veterans who served in ll wars and conflicts, distinguishing it from Memorial Day, which specifically remembers those who died while in service.

Veterans Day honors all living and deceased men and women who have served in the United States Armed Forces.

It is observed on November 11th, regardless of what day of the week on which it falls. When it was originally signed into law in 1968, with three other national holidays— Washington’s Birthday (Presidents Day), Memorial Day, and Columbus Day (Discovers Day) — all four were established to be three-day weekends for Federal employees to celebrate on a Monday.

According to the Veterans Affairs website, “It was thought that these extended weekends would encourage travel, recreational and cultural activities and stimulate greater industrial and commercial production.”

However, it was restored to be observed on November 11 (no matter which day it fell on) in 1975 by President Gerald R. Ford, returning the annual observance of Veterans Day to its original date of November 11, beginning in 1978. It is now observed on the day the date falls.

This action, according to Veteran Affairs, supported the desires of the overwhelming majority of state legislatures, all major veterans service organizations and the American people to preserve the historical significance of the date.

It also helps focus attention on the important purpose of Veterans Day: A celebration to honor America’s veterans for their patriotism, love of country, and willingness to serve and sacrifice for the common good.

## [S. Korea, US top diplomats discuss N. Korea, bilateral issues in Paris](https://www.koreatimes.co.kr/foreignaffairs/others/20261110/s-korea-us-top-diplomats-discuss-n-korea-bilateral-issues-in-paris?utm_source=rss)

via Korea Times · 2026-11-10

Foreign Minister Cho Hyun met with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio in France on Tuesday to discuss North Korea and bilateral issues, Seoul's foreign ministry said. Cho held a pull-aside meeting with Rubio on the sidelines of a Group of Seven (G7) foreign ministers' meeting and "exchanged views on overall bilateral relations, high-level exchanges and North Korea-related issues," the ministry said, without disclosing other details. Tuesday's meeting marked the first in-person encounter between the two foreign ministers since the results of the U.S. midterm elections were announced on Nov. 4. The meeting came as the South Korean Cabinet approved a bill earlier in the day seeking parliamentary consent for the government's plan to expand the operational scope of its anti-piracy Cheonghae unit from waters off the Somali coast to areas closer to the Strait of Hormuz. U.S. President Donald Trump has called on South Korea and other countries to help secure the vital waterway, which remains effectively blocked amid the U.S.-Iran war.

## [Army howitzer collides with civilian cars in fatal highway pileup crash](https://www.koreatimes.co.kr/southkorea/society/20261110/army-howitzer-collides-with-civilian-cars-in-fatal-highway-pileup-crash?utm_source=rss)

via Korea Times · 2026-11-10

An Army self-propelled howitzer collided with two civilian cars trailing from behind on a national highway in the central border region of Cheorwon last week, leaving one civilian driver dead, military officials said Tuesday. ## [National STEM Day encourages learning in science, technology, engineering and mathematics](https://www.samoanews.com/local-news/national-stem-day-encourages-learning-science-technology-engineering-and-mathematics)

via Samoa News · 2026-11-09

[![](https://www.samoanews.com/sites/default/files/styles/slideshow/public/field/image/national_stem_day.jpg?itok=qVlUcIRJ)](https://www.samoanews.com/sites/default/files/styles/article_normal_image/public/field/image/national_stem_day.jpg?itok=14YruYed)

_Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA —_ National STEM Day was celebrated yesterday, November 8 to encourage kids to explore their interests in the core subjects — science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM). The observance traces back to 2015 when a toy company aimed to inspire kids to pursue STEM fields through play.

Congresswoman Congresswoman Uifa'atali Aumua Amata’s office released the following statement on the yearly event:

As the global economy continues to grow and technology brings our world closer together, STEM education is more important than ever. Thank you to our educators in American Samoa helping to ensure our students have the knowledge and skills necessary to compete in an increasingly technology-driven world. Math and science education are driving forces for the future of business, innovation, and our economy.

Pacific Islanders have an excellent opportunity to advance in STEM fields. These careers are not limited to major cities, offering our students the opportunity to contribute to the global workforce while remaining connected to their island communities. We must ensure that our children here are not being left behind by increasing opportunities to explore their abilities in Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics in our local schools.

I am committed with you to ensuring that the youth of American Samoa are afforded the same opportunities and resources as their counterparts in the states, at every level from Head Start and elementary schools to high school and college. I look forward to continuing to work with our territory’s education leaders and my colleagues in Congress to support STEM education and prepare the next generation for the opportunities ahead.

This year, Congress designated $3 million of the growing American Samoa operations fund at my request to support needs at ASCC, and our bill (the Territorial Student Access to Higher Education Act, H.R. 6472) to provide students from the territories with in-state rates for university tuition is closer than ever. We’ve worked on this education policy for years, secured House-wide bipartisan support, and I will continue working for final passage.

The American Community Survey estimates that more than 41.6 million Americans ages 25 and older held a bachelor’s degree or higher in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics or a related field in 2025, representing roughly 47 percent of all people with a bachelor’s degree or higher.

## [POSCO union votes down tentative wage deal](https://www.koreatimes.co.kr/business/companies/20261107/posco-union-votes-down-tentative-wage-deal?utm_source=rss)

via Korea Times · 2026-11-07

Unionized workers at Korean steelmaker POSCO on Saturday voted down a tentative wage agreement reached with management that includes a 2.6 percent increase in base pay, union officials said. The vote showed 51.69 percent of the unionized workers opposed the wage agreement, while 48.31 percent approved it, according to the union. The tentative wage deal includes a 2.6 percent hike in base pay, a one-off payment of 6 million won ($4,500) and improved benefits. The union had initially demanded a 7.1 percent increase in base pay, a performance bonus equivalent to 600 percent of base pay, 50 company shares per worker and a holiday bonus equivalent to 200 percent of base pay. "We will probably need to open renegotiations as there were many opposing votes," a union official said. The union and management reached a tentative wage agreement on Oct. 30 after holding about 30 rounds of talks since June. Unionized POSCO workers staged two rounds of partial strikes in September to demand higher wages and bonuses.

SEYMEN, Turkey — In the countryside west of Istanbul, trucks line up to empty mixed household waste from the city of 16 million people onto a vast landscape of decomposing rubbish, where landfill gas is captured to generate electricity at a nearby plant. ## [Why Lee Chang-dong's award-winning 'Possible Love' struggled to find investors](https://www.koreatimes.co.kr/entertainment/films/20261107/why-lee-chang-dongs-award-winning-possible-love-struggled-to-find-investors?utm_source=rss)

Director Lee Chang-dong's "Possible Love" has earned international acclaim, winning the Silver Lion Grand Jury Prize at the 83rd Venice International Film Festival and securing invitations to major film festivals worldwide. Yet behind its remarkable success lies an uncomfortable reality: The film nearly never got made because it could not attract enough investment. The acclaimed project, released on Netflix on Friday, highlights a growing problem in the Korean film industry, where even internationally respected filmmakers and star-studded casts can struggle to secure financing. "Possible Love" follows two married couples whose lives intersect through the making of a documentary. ## [Pacific Horizons School receives donation from the Lealaifuaneva Peter E. Reid Charitable Foundation](https://www.samoanews.com/local-news/pacific-horizons-school-receives-donation-lealaifuaneva-peter-e-reid-charitable)

via Samoa News · 2026-11-06

[![Pacific Horizons receives Reid Foundation funds](https://www.samoanews.com/sites/default/files/styles/slideshow/public/field/image/phs_and_reid_foundation_donation_2026.jpg?itok=qh_j_moi)](https://www.samoanews.com/sites/default/files/styles/article_normal_image/public/field/image/phs_and_reid_foundation_donation_2026.jpg?itok=7xba55rW)

_Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA —_ Pacific Horizons School (PHS) is pleased to announce receiving a generous $20,000 donation from the Lealaifuaneva Peter E. Reid Charitable Foundation in support of the PHS 2nd Annual Giving Campaign. This contribution represents a significant investment in the school’s mission to provide high-quality educational opportunities for students in American Samoa.

The PHS Annual Giving Campaign was launched in 2025 to help secure the school’s long-term future amid changes to federal Consolidated Grant funding. This grant offset approximately 15% of the school’s operating costs. With restrictions now in place, PHS faces a deficit that poses challenges to maintaining its programs.

The Giving Campaign invites community partners to serve as “Anchor Donors,” aligning with the school’s nautical theme, by helping PHS reach its $70,000 goal. This support will directly strengthen the school’s general fund and ensure continued access to high-quality, well-rounded education for future generations.

Pacific Horizons School extends its warmest thanks to the Lealaifuaneva Peter E. Reid Charitable Foundation for its partnership and philanthropy. Their support helps make it possible for PHS to continue building a strong, innovative, and student-centered future.

For more information about the PHS Annual Giving Campaign or ways to support, please contact Veronica Soto, School Director at [veronicasoto@pacific-horizons-school.com](mailto:veronicasoto@pacific-horizons-school.com) (684) 699-5787.

## [EU tightens rules for baby formula after toxin scare](https://www.koreatimes.co.kr/world/20261106/eu-tightens-rules-for-baby-formula-after-toxin-scare?utm_source=rss)

via Korea Times · 2026-11-06

BRUSSELS — The European Union on Friday announced tighter health safety rules for baby formula following a contamination scandal involving cereulide, a toxin which can cause severe vomiting in newborns. The 27 member states approved the introduction of a "permanent food safety criterion for cereulide in infant formula", the European Commission said in a statement. In December 2025 food giant Nestle recalled dozens of infant formula batches in around 60 countries over the potential presence of the toxin. Similar recalls by manufacturers including Danone and Lactalis followed, up to April 2026. The EU said the contamination originated from the use of a Chinese-imported ingredient, an oil containing arachidonic acid. The presence of cereulide in products resulted from "deficiencies in the production process," the EU Commission's statement said. "Member states have approved strict maximum safety limits for the presence of the toxin in dried and liquid products."

MOMBASA, Kenya (AP) — The leader of a Kenyan doomsday cult linked to the deaths of more than 400 people was sentenced on Friday to 200 years in prison for the murders of 191 people. The High Court in Kenya’s coastal city of Mombasa issued the sentence for Pastor Paul Mackenzie. He was convicted of murdering 190 children and one adult after he ordered his followers to starve themselves to death in order to meet Jesus. Justice Diana Kavedza said that Mackenzie, leader of the Good News International Church, bore the “primary criminal culpability” for relocating his followers to a remote location and ordering them to fast to death. Mackenzie was charged with the murders alongside 28 of his followers, including guards who enforced his fasting directives and gravediggers who helped conceal the mass graves. All denied the charges, except for one person who confessed and pleaded for leniency. On Oct. 19, the court found all 29 of the accused guilty of the murder of 191 people. South Korean cryptocurrency exchange GOPAX said Friday it had suspended withdrawals as an emergency measure following hacking threats. The exchange said it halted withdrawals at 2:55 p.m. and was transferring most of the assets held in its so-called hot wallets to cold wallets, which are not connected to the internet. The precautionary measure was taken in response to hacking threats, and no actual loss of assets had been reported, GOPAX said. The South Korean financial sector has recently been hit by a series of cybersecurity incidents. The Financial Services Commission earlier said cybersecurity incidents had been confirmed at 37 financial institutions, affecting approximately 470,000 customer records.

I got the call in the summer of 1977, after applying to the U.S. Peace Corps to serve overseas as a volunteer. The application form allowed us to cite three countries in which we thought we might like to serve. I listed Nepal, Kenya and (a throwaway choice for fun in the sun) the Caribbean. Peace Corps headquarters told me that no openings were available in those places; would Afghanistan do instead? I hit my mental pause button, went camping for a weekend and checked back in with Peace Corps HQ. Afghanistan was no longer available; how about Korea? Thinking it was now or never, I took the plunge. Apart from the TV series “M\*A\*S\*H” and the thought that my favorite baseball player, Ted Williams of the Boston Red Sox, had flown several combat missions during the 1950-53 Korean War, I knew virtually nothing about Korea. ## [Inside look at 4-year mission behind Captain Q's unexpected resurgence](https://www.koreatimes.co.kr/southkorea/20261106/inside-look-at-4-year-mission-behind-captain-qs-unexpected-resurgence?utm_source=rss)

via Korea Times · 2026-11-06

Behind the unexpected resurgence of Captain Q, which returned to the liquor market after an 11-year hiatus, was one man's four-year mission to reinvent the brand. His goal was to make the inexpensive rum-based spirit — once notorious for hangovers so severe that drinkers joked it took two days to recover — appealing to younger consumers without the baggage of its past. Priced at less than 10,000 won ($7.20), Captain Q has returned to public notice with a viral advertising campaign featuring comedian Lee Sun-min that paid homage to 1980s commercials. Visitation 9-10:30 a.m. Friday, Nov. 13, at Dodo Mortuary Chapel. Celebration of life at 10:30 a.m. Inurnment to follow at East Hawaii Veterans Cemetery No. 2. Casual attire. Survived by wife, Ruth Y. Castillo of Hilo; stepchildren, Jennifer (Kevin) Nakano of Keaau, Gaven (Shelley) Fukunaga and Grant (Alise) Fukunaga of Hilo; sisters-in-law, Katherine (Keith) Higa of Hilo and Barbara (Charles) Bostwick of Molokai; brothers-in-law, Michael (Laurel) Matsuda of Waimea, Richard Weiser Jr. of Hilo, Dan (Jonnie) Weisgerber and Leon (Kristi) Weiser of Waimea, Franklin (Wendy) Weiser of Waikoloa; caregivers, Romeo and Helen Sembran of Hilo; 11 grandchildren and two great-grandchildren; nieces and nephews. Canada classifies trading profits as either capital gains or business income. For capital gains, only half the profit is included in taxable income. ## [TBS ATM machine now available at the airport](https://www.samoanews.com/local-news/tbs-atm-machine-now-available-airport)

via Samoa News · 2026-11-04

[![TBAS ATM Machine](https://www.samoanews.com/sites/default/files/styles/slideshow/public/field/image/airport_atms.png?itok=XcG85VWn)](https://www.samoanews.com/sites/default/files/styles/article_normal_image/public/field/image/airport_atms.png?itok=Y82AypP2)

Source: PAAS press release

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — Port Administration American Samoa (PAAS) has announced the opening of a Territorial Bank of American Samoa (TBAS) Automated Teller Machine (ATM) at Pago Pago International Airport, providing travelers, airport employees, and the general public with convenient access to banking services.

PAAS considers the new ATM as another positive step in Port Admin's ongoing efforts to improve airport facilities, enhance customer convenience, and deliver a better overall experience for residents and visitors traveling through American Samoa's primary international gateway.

Port Director Barney Sene expressed his appreciation to TBAS Chief Executive Officer Owen Peery and his team for recognizing the public need and working collaboratively with Port Administration to make this service available.

“We sincerely thank TBAS CEO Owen Peery and his entire team for recognizing this important public need and responding with a practical solution,” he said.

“Improving the airport experience is not just about major infrastructure investments. It is also about providing the everyday services and conveniences that make travel easier for our residents and visitors.”

Sene added, “Our goal is to make Pago Pago International Airport more welcoming, convenient, and responsive to the needs of the people we serve. We appreciate TBAS stepping forward as a partner in that effort and look forward to continued collaboration.”

## [ASCC Ethnomusicology Forum showcases SOLFA string ensemble](https://www.samoanews.com/local-news/ascc-ethnomusicology-forum-showcases-solfa-string-ensemble)

via Samoa News · 2026-11-04

“From Kitara to Orchestra: Mapping the String Traditions of Samoa”

[![Members of  SOLFA](https://www.samoanews.com/sites/default/files/styles/slideshow/public/field/image/ascc_ethnomusicology_2.jpeg?itok=8Rnp94yK)](https://www.samoanews.com/sites/default/files/styles/article_normal_image/public/field/image/ascc_ethnomusicology_2.jpeg?itok=EarJIgF8)

By

James Kneubuhl, ASCC Press Officer

_Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA  —_ The Fine Arts Department at the American Samoa Community College (ASCC) hosted its 5th annual Ethnomusicology Forum on Wednesday, October 28th. Intended to stimulate student interest, the forum typically explores some aspect of Music studies particularly relevant to the field.

The theme of this year’s forum was “From Kitara to Orchestra: Mapping the String Traditions of Samoa”, and the discussion traced the evolution of SOLFA, a string ensemble and music education group based in the Independent State of Samoa that seeks to integrate a western classical music approach with Samoan musical traditions.

To help set the stage for the event, on the day before the forum three members of SOLFA performed a late afternoon mini-concert for the ASCC students and staff.

Featured performers included Rosaivitilesaualofaoleola “Rosa” Solomona, co-founder and president of Solfa, on vocals and violin; Rosa’s brother Philton Solomona on violin and saxophone; and Haydon Afele-Nickel on violin.

The three musicians gave ensemble as well as solo performances, with a repertoire ranging from classical pieces to Samoan melodies, showcasing how easily music from different cultural contexts can co-exist within a single performance.

While only three of its musicians participated in the mini-concert and forum at ASCC, SOLFA regularly collaborates with many other players and singers in Samoa and beyond, and is equally adept at performing in either a small or a large-sized configuration.

At the forum itself, to give a broad overview of the history of western string instruments in relation to the music of Samoa, the forum presentation was divided into segments, the first of which was “Migration & Adaptation: The Arrival of the Strings”.

This section highlighted the arrival of the guitar and ukulele in Samoa via sailors, traders and missionaries, beginning a long integration process with the culture of Samoa. Keynote speaker Susau Konousi Solomona (mother of Rosa and Philton), Lecturer of Music & Performing Arts in the Faculty of Education at the National University of Samoa, shared insights based on many years of study, including anecdotes of the limited introduction of violins to Samoa by missionaries in the 1800s.

Next, the focus of the forum shifted to the present day for “The Genesis, Legacy and Politics of SOLFA”, for which Rosa Solomona served as guest speaker and recounted the formation and early activities of the string ensemble. Envisioning a group that could combine western music education with local cultural interests, Solomona found that bringing those two worlds together often required political negotiations, regional representation, and community support. Nevertheless, Solomona managed to work through the challenges, and in only a few years SOLFA established itself as a credible artistic and cultural entity.

The final portions of the forum consisted of a question-and-answer exchange, followed by a musical finale in which the SOLFA musicians collaborated with the ASCC Vocal Ensemble.

ASCC Fine Arts Department chairperson Mr. Kuki Tuiasosopo subsequently deemed the forum a success and thanked all of those who participated. “Fa’afetai tele lava colleagues,” said Tuiasosopo, “community members, and especially our students who joined us on Tuesday evening’s free concert and yesterday’s Ethnomusicology Forum!  Thank you for your support of our efforts.”

Tuiasosopo also credited local collaborators for their role in organizing SOLFA’s visit to American Samoa.

“We are deeply grateful for the wonderful partnership and collaboration with the Arts Council Executive Director Ammon Fepulea’i, Music Coordinator John Mailo, and Program Director Magdalene Leauanae of DOE Division of Curriculum and Instructions,” he said. “Together, we share a vision to preserve, perpetuate, and strengthen our Samoan musical heritage for the future generation.

“Bringing SOLFA on campus has reignited an interest among our students in Samoan instrumental music.  Therefore, we are committed to revive our instrumental ensembles, and working alongside the arts council and DCI, the future looks brighter for MUS 170 Beginning Orchestra, and MUS 180 Band.”

For more information on SOLFA, visit their pages on Facebook or Instagram, or their web page at: [https://solfamusic.org](https://solfamusic.org)

[![zoning board visit](https://www.samoanews.com/sites/default/files/styles/slideshow/public/field/image/img_7446.jpg?itok=VaNH98Vi)](https://www.samoanews.com/sites/default/files/styles/article_normal_image/public/field/image/img_7446.jpg?itok=FI3vzZK_)

By

Asi Andrew Fa'asau

andrew@samoanews.com

_Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA —_ For the second time in just over a year, local construction company Continental Transport Corporation (CTC) has been denied permission by the American Samoa Zoning Board to establish its retail and production operations at a new location.

The latest rejection came after the board voted to deny CTC's zoning variance application for a site in Tula, where the company had proposed relocating its operations after failing to secure approval for an earlier proposal in Leone.

CTC's planned operation included the retail sale, hauling, and storage of cinders, sand, rock aggregates, and other construction materials. The company also sought approval for laboratory testing of construction materials, rental of heavy equipment, truck and heavy machinery maintenance and repair services, and the manufacture of concrete and construction products.

With its administrative offices located in Pava'ia'i, CTC operated for more than a decade from its former production and retail headquarters in Fogagogo near Maliu Mai Beach Resort.

However, that chapter came to an end in 2025 when the company's lease expired and was not renewed.

After losing its Fogagogo location, CTC sought alternative sites from which to continue its operations. Company officials reportedly applied for space at the government-owned Daniel K. Inouye Industrial Park in Tafuna but were informed that no suitable lots were available.

The only government-owned property available at the time was a tract of land in Vailoa, Leone, commonly known as the "Airstrip."

CTC subsequently sought zoning approval to operate from the Airstrip property, but the proposal generated widespread opposition from nearby residents.

The site is surrounded by residential neighborhoods and is located near Leone High School, Leone Midkiff Elementary School, the Western District Health Center, the Leone Police Substation, and numerous family homes.

Residents packed public hearings before the Zoning Board, voicing concerns about dust, noise, heavy truck traffic, environmental impacts, and potential health risks. Written objections were also submitted to board members.

The strong community opposition ultimately played a significant role in the Zoning Board's decision to deny the Leone application in August of last year.

Undeterred by that setback, CTC returned to the Zoning Board last month seeking approval for a new site in Tula.

The proposed location sits on communal land belonging to the extended family of company owner Tony Togia'i.

Appearing on behalf of her husband, who was off-island at the time, Mrs. Togia'i told board members that the family had granted permission and fully supported the company's plans to establish a brick-manufacturing operation on the property.

She said CTC had gone to considerable lengths to gain community support before submitting its application.

According to Mrs. Togia'i, the company met with families living near the proposed site and received their approval. She submitted a petition bearing the signatures of those who supported the project.

She also informed the board that CTC had already invested substantial sums in specialized equipment, including a brick-manufacturing machine, and had constructed a purpose-built building designed to contain noise produced by the operation.

Mrs. Togia'i emphasized that brick production would only occur during designated daytime hours to minimize disturbance to neighboring residents.

Toward the end of last month, Zoning Board members Jim McGuire and Fofoga Sagato conducted a site inspection of the proposed Tula facility.

During their visit, they observed that there appeared to be no residences immediately adjacent to the operation.

Company owner Tony Togia'i accompanied the board members and explained the scope of the project. He also indicated that only one neighboring resident remained opposed to the operation.

The following day, McGuire visited that resident, Falaula Silivelio Vaoesea Aofia, to hear firsthand the concerns that had prompted his objection.

In an interview witnessed by Samoa News, Aofia described a very different picture of life next to the proposed CTC operation.

The retired U.S. Army veteran said construction activities on the site began approximately two years ago and involved extensive excavation work, heavy machinery activity, and large-scale earthmoving operations.

According to Aofia, the work has significantly affected the quality of life for his family.

"The breeze that comes from the ocean side of the village blows directly toward our home," Aofia explained. "When they operate the heavy machinery, the cement mixers, and the brick-making equipment, the noise is loud and the wind carries large amounts of dust toward our house."

He said the situation has become particularly difficult because of existing health conditions affecting both him and his wife.

"The air we breathe has become unsafe," he said. "It aggravates respiratory problems and prevents us from opening our windows or spending time outside."

Aofia noted that his wife is wheelchair-bound and suffers from respiratory ailments that could be worsened by dust generated by the operation.

He added that he also faces numerous health challenges and receives full medical benefits through the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs.

Aofia stated that he suffers from Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) resulting from his military service and said the constant noise from heavy equipment can trigger anxiety and stress.

The retired veteran also expressed frustration about how information regarding the project was communicated to residents.

Aofia said he believed he should have been informed much earlier about the proposal before it reached the Zoning Board.

He specifically questioned why the village pulenu'u had not made greater efforts to notify residents about a project that could directly affect their lives.

His frustration intensified when he reviewed the petition submitted by CTC in support of the application.

According to Aofia, he recognized many of the names on the document, including the signature of the village pulenu'u, who is also his first cousin.

Another signature that drew his attention belonged to a neighbor employed by the Department of Health.

Aofia said he had previously asked the individual to report what he viewed as health concerns associated with the operation to appropriate authorities.

Visibly upset, Aofia questioned how so many people who were familiar with his family's concerns had nevertheless signed the petition supporting the project.

Last Friday, as the Zoning Board met in executive session to make final decisions on pending variance applications, Aofia made an unexpected appearance.

To the surprise of several board members, he personally delivered a formal written complaint detailing his objections to the CTC operation.

Aofia explained that he had learned of the meeting through board members who had visited the site and felt compelled to ensure that his concerns were placed on the record before a final decision was made.

After considering the matter, board members voted to deny CTC's zoning variance application.

The decision marks the second unsuccessful attempt by the company to secure a new location for its operations following the loss of its longtime Fogagogo site, leaving the future location of one of the Territory's largest construction-material suppliers uncertain.
